keyVerseText: A land wherein thou shalt eat bread without scarceness, thou shalt not lack any thing in it; a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills thou mayest dig brass.
rootMeaning: The root of מִסְכֵּנֻת (miçkênuth) comes from מִסְכֵּן (miçkên), which denotes a poor or indigent person. This connection highlights that the noun form does not merely indicate a general lack, but specifically the condition or state of poverty and scarcity experienced by the poor. The root sense enriches the English gloss 'scarceness' by emphasizing the lived reality of deprivation and need inherent in poverty.
usageInScripture: The word מִסְכֵּנֻת occurs only once in Scripture, appearing in Deuteronomy 8:9. It is translated as 'scarceness' in this context, underscoring a lack or insufficiency that contrasts with the abundance promised in the land. This singular occurrence suggests a focused and precise use, pointing to the absence of poverty or shortage in the land God provides to His people.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מִסְכֵּנֻת as the condition of scarcity or poverty deepens our appreciation of God's provision and faithfulness. It reminds believers that God’s covenant blessings include deliverance from want, highlighting His role as provider. This word also gently confronts the reality of human need and dependence on divine grace, encouraging trust in God’s sufficiency. Theologically, it points to the spiritual and material abundance found in God’s kingdom, where poverty and lack are overcome through His sustaining power in Christ.
keyVerseReflection: Deuteronomy 8:9 states, 'A land wherein thou shalt eat bread without scarceness, thou shalt not lack any thing in it.' Here, מִסְכֵּנֻת (scarceness) conveys the absence of poverty or deficiency in the promised land. This word enriches the verse by emphasizing the completeness and sufficiency of God's provision, assuring His people that their basic needs will be fully met, reflecting His covenantal faithfulness and care.
